Getting started with knittogether

knittogether lets you work seamlessly with colleagues who write in Word or PowerPoint, while you keep analytic content reproducible in R and Quarto.

The core idea is:

  • Your colleagues write content in Office (Word/PPT)
  • You add placeholders where R-generated content should go
  • knittogether converts the document → markdown
  • You replace placeholders with R output (plots, tables, inline values)
  • You knit back to Word, PPT, PDF, HTML, or any Quarto format
  • If needed, the resulting Office document can be edited again and re-imported

A typical workflow looks like this:

Office (docx/pptx)

↓ convert Markdown + media/ folder

↓ clean Markdown (structured + tidy)

↓ replace Markdown (with R output inserted)

↓ render Quarto output (pptx, docx, html, pdf)

↓ optional Edit in Office

→ repeat

A minimal example

Suppose your colleague gives you a Word document with text and the following placeholders: placeholder_content_plot, which should contain a plot of your data, and placeholder_content_total_rows, which should give a count of the number of rows in your data.

1. Convert Word to markdown

First we [convert_markdown()] the docx file into a markdown file, extracting the contents and structure as well as images, tables, and citations.

knittogether::convert_markdown(
  input_file    = "input.docx",
  markdown_file = "report.md",
  media_base_dir = "media"
)

2. Clean the markdown

Next we clean_markdown() the resulting markdown so that it will be processed correctly by Quarto.

clean_markdown(
  markdown_file   = "report.md",
  heading_offset  = TRUE,
  clean_citations = TRUE
)

3. Create R-generated content

We then define the content (define_content()) we want to replace the placeholders with and map it to the placeholders (placeholder_map()) so we know what code matches what placeholder.

plot <- define_content(
  description    = "A scatterplot",
  placeholder_id = "plot",
  output_mode    = "chunk",
  content        = { plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width) },
  content_type   = "plot",
  chunk_options  = list(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6)
)

rows <- define_content(
  description    = "Number of rows in mtcars",
  placeholder_id = "total_rows",
  output_mode    = "inline",
  content        = { nrow(mtcars) },
  content_type   = "text"
)

content_map <- placeholder_map(specs = list(plot, rows))

4. Replace placeholders with real content

Next we replace_placeholders() the placeholders with this content and, optionally, validate the content is correct.

replace_placeholders(
  markdown_file      = "report.md",
  code_content       = content_map,
  placeholder_prefix = "placeholder_content",
  validation_path    = "validation"
)

If desired the markdown string can be passed to accessibility_scan() to check whether alt text or captions are present for all images and tables.

5. Render the Quarto document

Finally, we can render the resulting file into whatever format we want to output from Quarto. In your .qmd (e.g., report.qmd), include: {{{ < include report.md > }}} and then render with quarto::quarto_render("report.qmd"). Or, [replace_placeholders()] invisibly returns the contents of the markdown so it can be inserted directly into a Quarto file.

If you don’t want to run each step individually you can use run_workflow() to run them all at once. Each step reads the output of the step before it. Pass a folder as input_file to use its newest Word file, optionally narrowed with base_name. See the Working with versions section of the README for keeping earlier versions.

A fuller, ready-to-run example is provided in vignette("extended-workflow"). Other vignettes provide guidance on working with PowerPoint, citations, and setting up Office document styling.

Concepts

Understanding a few core ideas helps make sense of the workflow.

Placeholders

Placeholders are unique strings in Word or PowerPoint that indicate where R-generated content should go. For example placeholder_content_plot.

They have two parts:

  • prefix: This is shared across all placeholders and identifies that it is to be replaced (e.g., "placeholder_content")
  • identifier: This tells knittogether which content to replace it with ("plot")

Placeholders must use a shared prefix and should be unlikely to appear accidentally. They do not have to be unique if the same content is needed in multiple places.

Defining and mapping content

define_content() tells knittogether what to insert and how to insert it. Content can either be a single scalar (e.g. a number or string) which are inserted inline or a chunk (e.g. a plot, table, child Quarto document, or code block) which are inserted on a new line.

placeholder_map() combines all content definitions into a single object ready to replace the placeholders in the document.

When defining large or complex content it is advisable to use functions or ‘child’ documents and using the includes feature of Quarto. Important considerations for doing this are:

  • Keeping parent .qmd, child files, and markdown output in the same directory to avoid filepath issues when rendering.
  • Avoiding YAML in the child files where it may conflict with the parent document (e.g., format).
  • Ensuring data required by children or functions is available in the environment they are rendered in.

These can be added to the content argument of [define_content()] as content= "{{< include child_plot.qmd >}}".

Working Iteratively

You may find yourself going back and forth between Quarto and Word/PowerPoint. To make this easier you can use use draft mode to show the output of the code while keeping the placeholders.

replace_placeholders(
  markdown_file    = "report.md",
  code_content     = content_map,
  draft_mode       = TRUE,
  draft_mode_prefix = "DRAFT_CONTENT_START",
  draft_mode_suffix = "DRAFT_CONTENT_END",
  marker_mode      = "hidden"
)

In Word, placeholders can be configured to a “hidden” character style can be shown/hidden using ¶ to aid readability as shown in vignette("office-styling").
